summary: Herod Antipas hears of Jesus, is perplexed by talk of John raised or Elijah returned, and keeps trying to see him.

context.title: Herod’s perplexity
paragraphs: Luke sets this scene between the sending out of the Twelve and their return, so what reaches Herod is probably news of their mission. [c1] Matthew and Mark follow it with the full story of John’s death, which Luke does not tell. [c2] He has already reported that Herod shut John up in prison. [c3]

This Herod is Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Peraea after his father’s death. [c4] John had condemned his marriage to Herodias, the wife of his half-brother Philip, and that cost John his life. [c5] Matthew and Mark have Herod himself say that John has risen; Luke gives the idea to others and leaves Herod uncertain. [c6]

The rumours echo hopes of the time: Malachi had promised that Elijah would be sent before the day of the Lord. [c7] Some also expected Jeremiah or another of the great prophets to return as a herald of the Messiah. [c8] The same three answers come back later in the chapter, when Jesus asks who the crowds say he is. [c9]

translationNotes.summary: Tetrarch first meant the ruler of a quarter of a region, but by now named any minor prince.
translationNotes.body: The word joins four and rule, and first meant the governor of a fourth part of a region. [c10] It later lost that strict sense and could name any petty prince over a modest territory. [c11] Luke, like Matthew, gives Antipas this exact title, while Mark calls him king. [c12]

translationNotes.summary: Diēporei pictures someone who tries every way through and finds none: complete perplexity.
translationNotes.body: Diaporeo means to be entirely at a loss, and in the New Testament only Luke uses it. [c13] Vincent explains it as going through the whole list of possible ways and finding no way out. [c14] Meyer describes a man who could reach no certainty at all about who Jesus was. [c15] English perplexed is right, but the Greek is stronger than a passing puzzle. [c13][c14]

translationNotes.summary: Elijah “appeared” rather than “was raised”, because Scripture says he was taken up without dying.
translationNotes.body: Luke says that John has been raised from the dead, but that Elijah has appeared. [c16] Commentators explain the change by Elijah’s being taken up to heaven without dying, so he could return without rising. [c17] Bengel notes that the verb stands midway between the words for rising used of John and of the old prophets. [c18]

translationNotes.summary: Herod “was seeking” to see Jesus, a wish Luke picks up again at the Passion.
translationNotes.body: The verb means he sought, not merely wished, and literally reads was seeking. [c19] Luke returns to this desire at the Passion, when Pilate sends Jesus to Herod and Herod is glad at last to see him. [c20] Just before, Herod says I beheaded John with an emphatic I, which commentators hear as the voice of a troubled conscience. [c21]

claims.text: Lk 9:7-9 stands between the mission of the Twelve (Lk 9:1-6) and their return (Lk 9:10), and what Herod heard most naturally refers to that mission.
Matthew and Mark follow this scene with the account of John the Baptist’s death, which Luke does not tell.
Luke has already reported, in Lk 3:19-20, that Herod the tetrarch shut John up in prison.
Herod the tetrarch was Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, and after his father’s death ruled Galilee and Peraea.
Antipas married Herodias, the wife of his half-brother Philip, and John’s remonstrances against this marriage led to his death.
In Matthew and Mark Herod himself expresses the belief that John has risen, while Luke attributes it to others and leaves Herod in suspense.
Mal 3:23 (4:5 in some Bibles) promises that Elijah the prophet will be sent before the day of the Lord, and the rumour about Elijah accords with this prophecy.
Jeremiah and other great prophets were looked for by some Jews as heralds of the coming Messiah.
In Lk 9:19 the disciples report the same three opinions: John the Baptist, Elijah, or one of the old prophets risen.
Τετράρχης (from τέτρα and ἄρχω) strictly means a governor of the fourth part of a region.
The word lost its strict etymological force and came to denote a petty prince over a territory of comparatively narrow limits.
Luke, like Matthew, calls Herod ὁ τετραάρχης, where Mark calls him βασιλεύς.
Διαπορέω means to be entirely at a loss, and in the New Testament only Luke uses it.
Vincent explains διαπορέω as going through the whole list of possible ways and finding no way out.
Meyer explains that Herod could not in the least arrive at certainty about the person of Jesus.
Luke uses ἠγέρθη (was raised) of John in Lk 9:7 but ἐφάνη (appeared) of Elijah in Lk 9:8.
Ἐφάνη is used of Elijah because he had not died but been taken up to heaven (2 Kgs 2:11).
Bengel notes that ἐφάνη is put midway between ἠγέρθη and ἀνέστη, the verbs used in Lk 9:7-8 of John and of the old prophets.
Ἐζήτει literally means “was seeking”: Herod did more than desire to see Jesus.
Luke returns to Herod’s desire in Lk 23:8, when Pilate sends Jesus to Herod on the day of the crucifixion.
The emphatic ἐγὼ in “I beheaded” (Lk 9:9) is read as the voice of a guilty, troubled conscience.
